competitors.name: Chessable (by Play Magnus / Chess.com)
competitors.model: Course marketplace + MoveTrainer PRO subscription add-on

pricing.freeTier: Basic MoveTrainer with restricted active course slots

strengths: Spaced repetition engine (MoveTrainer) reinforces memory retention
Author catalog features elite Grandmasters (Magnus Carlsen, Anish Giri, Daniel Naroditsky)
weaknesses: Bloated 40-hour opening courses memorizing 30-move theoretical variations opponents rarely play
Punishing and robotic UX that frustrates 800–1600 Elo adult improvers
Prioritizes rote memorization over dynamic tactical radar and piece protection instincts
customerComplaints: "MoveTrainer forces me to repeat 20 moves of opening theory my opponents never play."
"Video upgrades double or triple the cost to $100–$250 for content I barely finish."
"Felt like studying for a brutal exam rather than enjoying chess improvement."

competitors.name: Chessly (by GothamChess / Levy Rozman)
competitors.model: Annual/monthly subscription or standalone course purchases
strengths: Massive brand recognition through YouTube (GothamChess 5M+ subscribers)
weaknesses: Video-heavy: users spend hours passively watching rather than actively solving
High recurring subscription cost ($89.99/yr or $19.99/mo) and single course price ($69–$99)
Heavy emphasis on opening repertoires that low-rated opponents deviate from by move 3
Passive watching creates an 'illusion of competence' that evaporates during live rapid games
customerComplaints: "I watched 3 hours of video, felt confident, and hung a piece on move 8 in my next rapid game."
"$89.99/yr is steep for casual adult improvers with only 15 minutes a day."
"Felt like watching YouTube with a small quiz at the end rather than hands-on tactical training."

competitors.name: Chess.com Diamond
strengths: Native ecosystem where games are played with integrated Game Review
Unlimited tactical puzzles and bot matches
weaknesses: Puzzle system rapidly serves obscure multi-move deflections rather than basic pattern hygiene
Recurring $120/yr creates subscription fatigue and continuous churn
Lessons are brief disconnected video snippets without structured tactile habit-building
customerComplaints: "Game Review points out my blunders, but doesn't teach my brain how to spot them before clicking."
"Tired of paying $120/year when I only have 15 minutes on lunch breaks to practice."
"Puzzles jump from simple forks to complex Grandmaster deflections with zero guidance."

competitors.name: Aimchess
strengths: Connects to Chess.com/Lichess to pinpoint historical weaknesses
Generates customized tactical drills based on user game mistakes
weaknesses: Diagnostic rather than prescriptive: informs you of mistakes without rewiring real-time reflexes
Requires large game volume to generate statistically significant data
Adds another monthly recurring bill for passive statistical dashboards
customerComplaints: "Aimchess diagnosed that I blundered rooks, but didn't give me a structured habit to fix it."
"Another recurring monthly bill for analytics when what I need is tactile survival training."

marketSummary.highEndVideo: Chessable ($100–$300+) and Chessly ($69–$99 / $89.99/yr) dominate video courses but suffer low completion (<15%) and passive fatigue.
marketSummary.subscriptionFatigue: Chess.com Diamond ($120/yr) and Aimchess ($8–$15/mo) lock users into indefinite recurring billing without addressing the root cause of plateaus.
marketSummary.ourValidationTier: BlunderProof offers an accessible $49–$69 one-time lifetime tier or light $7.99/mo subscription, focused 100% on active blunder prevention and Checks-Captures-Threats (CCT).
